_shape: One feature built the spec-kit way. A spec member writes the spec, a plan reviewer runs analyze, one implementer runs implement.
_why_this_works: Spec-kit writes a spec, a plan and a task list before any code, and stops there: it runs no task in parallel and checks nothing itself. teamwire supplies the parts spec-kit leaves out: one worktree per writer, file ownership, a fresh reader before the build, independent checks and the merge. Each spec-kit command runs in the seat whose rules fit it, so spec-kit stays unchanged.
_input: A feature description from the user, or a finished `tasks.md` the user brings. With a finished `tasks.md` committed on a branch, leave out the spec member: the plan reviewer still runs `analyze` on it before any implementer starts, with its `cwd` at a checkout of that branch. Then start the implementer from that branch.
_rules: BEFORE. The base branch holds spec-kit, committed: `.specify/` and the command folder of each member harness (`specify init --here --force --integration claude`, then `specify integration install codex` or `pi`), and a written `.specify/memory/constitution.md`. A worktree holds only committed files. No spec-kit `git` extension (the `installed:` list in `.specify/extensions.yml`) and no spec-kit runtime event set up: no `.codex/config.toml` or `.codex/hooks.json` exists, `.claude/settings.json` has no hook tagged `"__speckit_event__": true`, and `.specify/` holds no events script for such hooks. An extension declares `events:` in its manifest, `.specify/extensions/<id>/extension.yml`, and `.specify/integration-events.yml` overrides them; a manifest whose events spec-kit wrote no hook for, such as a disabled extension, sets nothing up. No other extension has an enabled hook with `optional: false` in `.specify/extensions.yml`: every spec-kit command tells the member to run such a hook and wait for it, and a hook can demand a merged pull request or commit, push or switch branches. Clear each one before launch: read what it runs, then remove the extension or make the hook optional, then commit. teamwire owns the branches, Codex launch refuses a repository that holds `.codex/config.toml` or `.codex/hooks.json`, and an `events:` hook in `.claude/settings.json` runs unreviewed. Run `teamwire doctor --base <base>` from the repository, with the branch the first member starts from (default `HEAD`), and read its nine `spec-kit ...` lines: `spec-kit version`, `spec-kit committed`, `spec-kit constitution`, `spec-kit integrations`, `spec-kit git extension`, `spec-kit hooks`, `spec-kit events`, `spec-kit feature pointer` and `spec-kit workflows`. Each names the ref and its commit and reads that commit, the one a worktree is cut from. Each is `ok` or `warn`, and a `warn` names the file and one action that fixes it before launch. Do not git-ignore a command folder, although `specify init` advises ignoring `.claude/`: a worktree member then gets no spec-kit commands. `specify init` also installs a workflow, `.specify/workflows/speckit/workflow.yml`, listed in `.specify/workflows/workflow-registry.json`. Nothing runs it unless someone runs `specify workflow run`, and no teamwire member does. Read the section 'Spec-kit features' in the skill's `reference.md` first: it says what each `warn` means.

SPEC. The spec member stops once per batch of questions. It runs `specify` with the feature description and stops with its questions from `specify`, at most 3. `specify` ranks no option, so the member marks its own recommended option for each question and says the mark is its own. Ask the user and reprompt it with the answers. It writes them into `spec.md` the way `specify`'s own steps say: it replaces each `[NEEDS CLARIFICATION]` marker with its answer, re-runs `specify`'s validation, and ticks each item of `checklists/requirements.md` that now passes. Then it runs `clarify`'s scan, and stops again with clarify's questions, at most 5, each with clarify's recommended option. Ask the user and reprompt it again. `clarify` asks one question at a time in chat, so the member cannot run it with a batch of answers: it follows clarify's write steps by hand with your answers. Both batches go in clarify's `## Clarifications` section of `spec.md`, under `### Session YYYY-MM-DD`, one line per answer in clarify's format `- Q: <question> → A: <answer>`, so `spec.md` has one place for every answer. Then it runs `plan` and `tasks`, and commits after each command. A stop with no questions records no stop: when `specify` asks none, or `clarify`'s scan reports no critical ambiguities, the member goes on to the next command. A further stop is allowed only when an answer raises a new question. The member never answers a spec-kit question itself, unless your reprompt says to take the recommended option: the member's own mark at stop 1 and clarify's at stop 2. Then it lists each such answer under Decisions I made, with whose mark it took. At each stop it writes its questions under the heading 'Questions for the parent' in its report and records `teamwire done --status blocked --summary "3 questions for the parent. ..."` with its own count, or `1 question for the parent.` for one, because its check fails there. That `blocked` is a question round, not a failure: a result with status `blocked` whose summary, after an optional leading `handoff: `, matches `^[1-9][0-9]* questions? for the parent\.`. Its seat rules say to ask by question message and decide when no answer comes, so its brief carries the override line from 'Spec-kit features' in the skill's `reference.md`, word for word. It records `done` only after `tasks` is written and its check passes. The user reviews `spec.md` and `plan.md`. `specify` writes `checklists/requirements.md` itself and ticks each item that passes its validation; an item stays unticked while the spec holds a question, so check that this checklist has no unticked item before the review. The reviewer-only rule is about the `checklist` command's checklists: the user ticks those at this review, because only a reviewer may tick one. Then reprompt the spec member to commit them before any implementer starts, because a worktree holds only commits.

ONE SPEC AT A TIME. Run one spec member at a time and name its folder yourself, such as `specs/001-name/`. Spec-kit picks the next number by scanning `specs/`. Each spec member scans `specs/` in its own worktree, so two spec members on branches cut from the same base pick the same number, even when they run one after the other. Spec-kit issue #4270 is the related upstream report.

CHECK. Add the plan reviewer with `teamwire launch --add` after the spec member's last commit. Its `cwd` is the spec member's worktree, so it reads the committed spec. It runs `analyze`, which is read-only, and reads the briefs. It also runs any task in `tasks.md` that claims "confirm the new tests fail", in its own scratch copy under `$TEAMWIRE_SCRATCH`, outside the repository, because a claim that is half false can lead the implementer to weaken tests. Reprompt the spec member once with the findings that hold. Never run a second analyze on the same plan.

BUILD. One implementer by default. Before you write its spec, run `teamwire speckit draft specs/NNN-name/tasks.md` and show the user its table: the files phases and stories share, and the tasks that change no file or touch only their own files. Start the implementer's `owns` from the DRAFT lists, check each one, and grep for the names a draft cannot see. Its `base` is the spec member's branch, so the feature folder is in its worktree. Its `setup` writes `.specify/feature.json` with `{"feature_directory": "specs/NNN-name"}`, because spec-kit git-ignores that file and a new worktree has none. It runs `implement` phase by phase, ticks `[X]` only on its own phases' lines in `tasks.md`, commits at the end of every phase that has tasks, and reads the constitution. Each commit holds that phase's code and its ticks and names the task ids in the message. Spec-kit's `tasks.md` template writes a `**Checkpoint**` line after the Foundational phase and after each story phase, so Setup and Polish have none. A phase with no tasks, such as an empty Foundational phase, gets no commit. The brief overrides any commit line in the notes of `tasks.md`, such as the template's "Commit after each task or logical group" or a model's own "Commit after every checkpoint". `implement`'s ignore-file step appends spec-kit's critical patterns to `.gitignore` and may create other ignore files, so the brief says the implementer follows the ignore-file step for `.gitignore` only, appends only the patterns the step lists, lists each one it added in its report, and writes no other ignore file unless its brief owns that file. The brief also says a "confirm the tests fail" task is finished when the cases it names fail, and the implementer never changes a test to make it fail. Its `check` needs `tasks.md`, runs the tests and fails on any unticked task, such as `test -s specs/NNN-name/tasks.md && <tests> && ! grep -nE '^[[:space:]]*[-*+][[:space:]]+\[[[:space:]]*\][[:space:]]*T[0-9]+' specs/NNN-name/tasks.md`. Without the `test -s`, the grep check passes when the folder name is wrong, because `!` turns grep's missing-file error into success. The grep also catches an open task with extra spaces, a tab, an indent or a `*` or `+` bullet. The check still passes on a lowercase `[x]` or a deleted task line, so the closer counts the ticks (CLOSE).

Implement stops with 'Do you want to proceed with implementation anyway?' when a checklist has unticked items. So the stop fires only when a checklist has unticked items, such as one from `checklist` that the user left open, or an item of `specify`'s own `requirements.md` that is still unticked. The brief tells the implementer to treat that stop as a question to you.

SPEC AMENDMENT. Worktrees share no files. The implementer's branch is cut from the spec member's branch at launch, so it starts with the spec as committed then. After that only the spec member changes `spec.md`, `plan.md` and the design files, and it commits each change. Then the spec member itself announces the change to every running implementer and to you, with a notice that names the commit: `teamwire send <team> --to <implementers>,lead --type notice --commit <sha> --text "SPEC AMENDMENT: run 'git merge --no-ff --no-edit <sha>' now. <what changed and why>"`. `--no-ff` makes the merge a merge commit even before the implementer's first commit, so verify skips it. A fast-forward would make the spec member's commit look like the implementer's own, and verify and `done` would flag it. A notice must name a commit on the sender's branch, so it cannot point at uncommitted work. Uncommitted edits in the spec member's worktree never reach anyone. Each implementer's brief says: on a notice that starts with `SPEC AMENDMENT:`, merge that commit before your next unit, then go on. The lead sends nothing. verify does not flag the merged spec files for the one implementer or for a split's wave 1 member, because their `base` is the spec branch. Every other member of a split, such as a story member or the Polish or fix-round member, has a `base` that is not the spec branch, so verify flags each merged spec file as `outside-owns:specs/NNN-name/<file>`. Waive each such flag with the notice as the reason, such as `teamwire verify <team> --role <role> --waive outside-owns:specs/NNN-name/spec.md --reason "SPEC AMENDMENT notice m007"`. Once an implementer starts, only implementers write `tasks.md`: their ticks and the Convergence sections that converge appends. The spec member never edits `tasks.md` again, so the amendment merge cannot conflict on it.

SPLIT ONLY ON DISJOINT FILES. One implementer per user story only when the stories after the Foundational phase touch disjoint files. Decide from the `Stories that share files` line of `teamwire speckit draft`, and show the user that table and the split you recommend before you launch. Each story member's `owns` starts from its story's DRAFT list. Wave 1 is Setup and Foundational, wave 2 has one member per story, and Polish comes last. Each member owns `tasks.md` too and ticks only its own phase's lines, so launch warns that each pair of story members has overlapping `owns` on `tasks.md`: expect that warning, which refuses nothing, and keep `tasks.md` in every member's `owns`. Its `check` is `test -s specs/NNN-name/tasks.md && <its own tests>`, with no grep for unticked tasks. The integrator's `check` on the joined branch carries the whole-file grep instead. JOIN: the integrator (`teamwire preset integrator`) merges Foundational first, then the stories in priority order. Wave 1's branch is cut from the spec member's branch, so the integrator's diff from `main` holds every spec file and verify flags each one as `outside-owns:`: put `specs/NNN-name/` in the integrator's `owns`. The CLOSE rule says where the fix round runs in a split.

CLOSE. Start the closer from `teamwire preset closer` and add two steps to its task. First, it counts the ticks at each of the implementer's commits and checks that no task line is missing, because the implementer's check still passes on a lowercase `[x]` or a deleted task line. Second, in its own clone, write `.specify/feature.json` at the clone's root, read the clone's `converge` command file of any installed harness, such as `.claude/skills/speckit-converge/SKILL.md`, follow it with every script run from the clone's root, and report converge's findings table. The closer never invokes `/speckit-converge` from its own session, because that session starts in your checkout. The section converge appends to `tasks.md` stays in that clone. A finding in the spec's own words goes to the spec member first, because converge compares the code with the spec's text and so cannot find a gap that the spec itself carries. Then the fix round runs in this order: the spec member changes the spec and design files and commits, without touching `tasks.md`, and sends its SPEC AMENDMENT notice; the implementer merges that commit, then runs the loop. In the fix round, the one implementer runs `converge` on its own branch, then `implement` on the new phase, then `converge` again, and stops at "Converged" or after two rounds. Converge makes no commit, so the implementer commits converge's appended section alone, before it implements it, with a message such as `converge round 1: ...`. In a per-story split, story owners run no `converge`, because converge compares the code with the whole spec and on a story branch reports every other story as `missing`. So in a split the fix round runs on a branch cut from the integrator's branch, by one implementer, such as the Polish member. It runs the same loop on the joined code and is the only writer of the Convergence phase. The integrator then merges its branch.

pi members do not load `.pi/prompts/`, because teamwire starts pi with `--no-approve` (ADR 0029). A pi brief says: read `.pi/prompts/speckit.<cmd>.md` and follow it, with `$ARGUMENTS` set to the scope.

AFK. An AFK run builds a spec-kit feature only from a `spec.md`, `plan.md` and `tasks.md` that the user already reviewed and committed, starting as for a finished `tasks.md` (input). The spec stage needs the user at both question stops, at the review of `spec.md` and `plan.md`, and for the `checklist` command's ticks, and an AFK lead would answer all of them itself.
REF. The team carries the feature as a ref, `{"provider": "speckit", "id": "NNN-name"}`, so `teamwire decisions --ref speckit:NNN-name` finds every team that worked on it.
title: CHANGEME spec-kit feature
setup: echo 'CHANGEME: fill in the worktree setup command' >&2; false

children._note: Launch alone first. Its check fails until `tasks.md` exists, so at each question stop it records `blocked`, and `done` only once `tasks` is written. Its brief names the folder, the spec-kit commands it runs in order, the questions rule, and the override line from the skill's `reference.md`, word for word, so its seat's "decide and finish" rule never answers a spec-kit question. Keep it open until the team closes: it fixes what analyze finds, and in the fix round it fixes a finding in the spec's own words. Its brief says to send the `SPEC AMENDMENT:` notice (rule SPEC AMENDMENT) after every commit that changes `spec.md`, `plan.md` or a design file once an implementer has started, and never to edit `tasks.md` after that.
children.title: Spec: CHANGEME
children.check: test -s specs/001-CHANGEME/spec.md && test -s specs/001-CHANGEME/plan.md && test -s specs/001-CHANGEME/tasks.md

children._launch_after: spec has committed tasks.md and the user has reviewed spec.md and plan.md
children._note: On Claude Code, give this member the plugins map from the skill's 'Skills and plugins in members', so it reads no other member's findings through memory.
children.title: Analyze the CHANGEME spec
children.task: Review the spec-kit feature specs/001-CHANGEME for team myteam before any implementer starts. Your directory is the spec member's worktree. Run spec-kit's analyze command for that feature (CHANGEME: `/speckit-analyze` on Claude Code, `$speckit-analyze` on Codex, or on pi read `.pi/prompts/speckit.analyze.md` and follow it). Analyze is read-only: do not accept its offer of edits. For every task in `tasks.md` that claims "confirm the new tests fail", run it in your own scratch copy of this worktree under `$TEAMWIRE_SCRATCH`, outside the repository, and report each case it names that does not fail. Then read the plan at /abs/path/briefs/PLAN.md, the team spec at /abs/path/briefs/spec.json and every brief in /abs/path/briefs/. For each brief, write what it asks the member to build. Report analyze's findings table, then each place where a member would have to decide, guess or ask, ranked by harm, each with its file and line. Findings only, no fixes. Do NOT edit any file in the repository. If the spec and every brief are ready, say so plainly rather than inventing findings. Start your report file with a summary of at most ten lines: the outcome, then what the lead must decide.

children._launch_after: the spec member has fixed analyze's findings and committed
children._note: Its base is the spec member's branch. Its setup writes `.specify/feature.json`. Its `owns` starts from the DRAFT lists of `teamwire speckit draft`, checked by you. Its brief names its phases, the tick rule, a commit at the end of every phase that has tasks with the task ids, the ignore-file rule, the rule for a "confirm the tests fail" task, the constitution, the checklist stop as a question to you, and the merge on a notice that starts with `SPEC AMENDMENT:`. For a Claude Code member with mattpocock-skills on, put these two sentences in the brief file: Use the tdd skill for each unit; test only at these seams: CHANGEME. If a check fails and the cause is not clear from its output, use the diagnosing-bugs skill before your second fix attempt.
children.title: Build: CHANGEME
children.setup: echo 'CHANGEME: fill in the worktree setup command' >&2; false && printf '%s\n' '{"feature_directory": "specs/001-CHANGEME"}' > "$1/.specify/feature.json"
children.check: test -s specs/001-CHANGEME/tasks.md && CHANGEME targeted test command && ! grep -nE '^[[:space:]]*[-*+][[:space:]]+\[[[:space:]]*\][[:space:]]*T[0-9]+' specs/001-CHANGEME/tasks.md
